relationship: parallel warning against human reliance in place of hope in God
rationale: Jeremiah curses reliance on a human when the heart departs from the Lord; the psalm warns against trusting rulers and human beings who cannot save, then blesses hope in God. The contrast concerns the object of trust, not a ban on every human relationship.
source_text: Cursed is the person who places his hope in a human and will rest the flesh of his arm upon him, and whose heart departs from the Lord;

target_units.text: Do not trust in rulers and in sons of men who have no salvation.
His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their reasonings will perish.
Happy the one whose Helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God,

relationship: same-chapter contrast between desolate and well-watered plants
rationale: The person relying on a human is compared to a wild tamarisk in an uninhabited salt wilderness. The following blessing compares the person trusting the Lord to a tree rooted beside water and continuing to bear fruit, forming the oracle's deliberate botanical contrast.
source_text: and he will be like a wild tamarisk in the wilderness; he will not see when good things come, and will dwell among salt-plants and in a wilderness, in a salt land that is not inhabited.

target_units.text: And blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope;

and he will be like a tree flourishing beside waters, and will send its roots toward moisture, and will not fear when heat comes. Wooded stems will be upon it; in a rainless year it will not fear or cease bearing fruit.

relationship: close blessing of the person whose hope is the Lord
rationale: Both explicitly pronounce blessing or happiness upon a person whose hope is in the Lord. The psalm further calls the God of Jacob that person's Helper.
source_text: And blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope;

target_units.text: Happy the one whose Helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God,

relationship: close image of the fruitful tree beside water
rationale: Both portray a favored person as a tree beside water that continues to bear fruit. Jeremiah expressly addresses heat and a rainless year; the psalm adds an unfailing leaf and prosperity in the person's actions.
source_text: and he will be like a tree flourishing beside waters, and will send its roots toward moisture, and will not fear when heat comes. Wooded stems will be upon it; in a rainless year it will not fear or cease bearing fruit.

target_units.text: He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

relationship: related depth of the human heart and difficulty of knowing it
rationale: Jeremiah calls the heart deep and asks who will know the human being; Proverbs compares counsel in a person's heart to deep water that an intelligent person draws out. The comparison preserves depth and discernment without importing a claim that Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful.
source_text: The heart is deep beyond all things, and so is a human; and who will know him?

target_units.text: Counsel in a man’s heart is deep water, but an intelligent man will draw it out.

relationship: close divine testing of hearts and kidneys
rationale: Jeremiah names the Lord as examiner of hearts and tester of kidneys; the psalm addresses God with the same paired inward testing. Both place that examination in a setting of distinguishing righteous and wicked conduct.
source_text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

target_units.text: Let sinners’ wickedness come to an end, and Thou wilt direct the righteous one, God who tests hearts and kidneys.

relationship: close repayment according to each person's deeds
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord gives each person according to his ways and the fruits of his practices; Romans says God repays each according to his works. This target supplies the explicit recompense clause, distinct from the heart-and-kidney imagery.
source_text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

target_units.text: who will repay each according to his works:

relationship: related adverse outcomes of unjustly acquired wealth
rationale: Jeremiah joins wealth made without judgment to abandonment in the middle of the possessor's days and final foolishness; Proverbs says property pursued with lawlessness diminishes. Proverbs does not reproduce the partridge image or Jeremiah's timing in the middle of the person's days.
source_text: A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear. One makes his wealth without judgment; in the middle of his days they will abandon him, and at his last he will be foolish.

target_units.text: Property pursued eagerly with lawlessness becomes less, but one who gathers for himself with piety will increase; a righteous person has compassion and lends.

relationship: related sanctuary as the place of God's throne
rationale: Jeremiah calls the sanctuary an exalted throne of glory. In Ezekiel's temple vision, God identifies the place of His throne and the footprints of His feet where His name will dwell among Israel.
source_text: An exalted throne of glory is our sanctuary,

target_units.text: He said to me, “Have you seen, son of man, the place of My throne and the place of the footprints of My feet, where My name will dwell among the house of Israel for ever? The house of Israel will no longer profane My holy name, neither they nor their rulers, by their prostitution and by the murders of the rulers among them—

relationship: close accusation of abandoning the divine fountain of life
rationale: Both passages condemn abandoning the Lord under the image of life-giving water. Jeremiah 2 develops the contrast with broken cisterns, whereas Jeremiah 17 asks shame upon those abandoning Him.
source_text: Israel’s patient expectation, Lord, let all who abandoned Thee be ashamed; let those who departed be written upon the earth, because they abandoned the Lord, the fountain of life.

target_units.text: For My people did two evil things: they abandoned Me, a spring of water of life, and dug broken cisterns for themselves that will not be able to hold water.

relationship: parallel appeal to the Lord for healing and salvation
rationale: Jeremiah asks the Lord to heal and save him; the psalm likewise asks divine healing and rescue. Jeremiah grounds the appeal in the Lord as his boast, while the psalm appeals to mercy amid bodily and inward distress.
source_text: Heal me, Lord, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, because Thou art my boast.

target_units.text: Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones were troubled,
and my soul was greatly troubled. And Thou, Lord—how long?
Return, Lord; rescue my soul. Save me for the sake of Thy mercy.

relationship: close challenge that the announced divine action should arrive
rationale: Jeremiah reports people asking where the Lord's word is and demanding that it come. Isaiah reports a comparable challenge that God's action and the Holy One's counsel should approach so the challengers can see and know.
source_text: Behold, they say to me: Where is the Lord’s word? Let it come!

target_units.text: who say, “Let what He will do approach quickly, so that we may see, and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, so that we may know!”

relationship: related appeal to God's knowledge of the speaker
rationale: Jeremiah appeals to the Lord's knowledge and places what proceeds from his lips before Him. The psalm speaks of divine testing and knowledge of the speaker's movements and reasonings, then mentions the tongue and God's knowledge of all things; it does not explain Jeremiah's unusual phrase about a human's day.
source_text: But I did not grow weary following after Thee, and did not desire a human’s day; Thou knowest. The things going out through my lips are before Thee.

target_units.text: For the end. A psalm for David. Lord, Thou didst test me and know me.
Thou knewest my sitting and my rising; Thou didst understand my reasonings from afar.
Thou didst trace my path and my measuring cord, and Thou didst foresee all my ways.
For there is no word on my tongue,
behold, Lord, Thou knewest all things, the last and the first; Thou didst form me and place Thy hand upon me.

relationship: parallel plea against divine estrangement during danger
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the Lord not become an estrangement to him in an evil day. The psalm asks God not to forsake or remain far from the speaker while enemies plot against him.
source_text: Do not become an estrangement to me, sparing me in an evil day.

target_units.text: Do not cast me away at the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me.
For my enemies spoke to me, and those watching my soul plotted together,
saying, “God has forsaken him! Pursue him and overtake him, for there is no rescuer!”
God, do not go far from me; my God, attend to my help!

relationship: parallel appeal for shame and reversal upon pursuers
rationale: Both ask that those pursuing or seeking the speaker's life be shamed and overtaken by judgment. Jeremiah asks double crushing; the psalm develops reversal through the enemies' own hidden trap.
source_text: Let those pursuing me be ashamed, and may I not be ashamed; may they be terrified, and may I not be terrified. Bring an evil day upon them; crush them with double crushing.

target_units.text: Let those who seek my soul be ashamed and abashed; let those devising evils for me turn backward and be put to shame.
Let them become like dust before the wind, with an angel of the Lord pressing them out.
Let their way become darkness and a slippery path, with an angel of the Lord pursuing them.
For without cause they hid for me the destruction of their trap; without purpose they reproached my soul.
Let a trap they do not know come upon them; let the snare they hid catch them, and into that trap they will fall.

relationship: related use of Jerusalem's gates for Sabbath regulation
rationale: Jeremiah is sent to the gates to deliver the Sabbath warning that follows. Nehemiah later stations servants at Jerusalem's gates and closes them so that Sabbath burdens will not pass through, giving a concrete counterpart to the location of Jeremiah's warning.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Go and stand in the gates of your people’s sons, through which Judah’s kings enter and leave, and in all Jerusalem’s gates,

target_units.text: When the gates of Jerusalem were at rest before the Sabbath, I gave orders and they closed the gates. I ordered that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. I stationed some of my young servants at the gates so that no burdens would be carried on the Sabbath day.

relationship: close royal and public summons at the gates
rationale: Both summonses address Judah's king or kings together with the people entering the gates and call them to hear the Lord's word. Their surrounding instructions differ: Sabbath observance here and royal justice in chapter 22.
source_text: and you will say to them: Hear the Lord’s word, kings of Judah, all Judea and all Jerusalem, who enter these gates:

target_units.text: and say: Hear the Lord’s word, king of Judah who sits on David’s throne—you, your household, your people, and those entering these gates.

relationship: close prohibition of Sabbath burdens at Jerusalem's gates
rationale: Jeremiah forbids lifting Sabbath burdens and going out through Jerusalem's gates. Nehemiah describes burdens brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath and orders the gates guarded against their passage; the directions of movement are not identical.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not lift burdens on the Sabbath day or go out through Jerusalem’s gates,

target_units.text: In those days I saw people in Jouda treading winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing sheaves and loading them on donkeys, with wine, grapes, figs and every kind of burden, bringing them to Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. I warned them on the day of their selling.
People lived there bringing fish and every kind of merchandise, selling on the Sabbath to the sons of Jouda and in Jerusalem.
I contended with the free men of Jouda and said to them, “What is this evil thing you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?
“Did not your fathers do this, so that our God brought all these evils upon them and upon us and upon this city? Yet you add wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath.”

When the gates of Jerusalem were at rest before the Sabbath, I gave orders and they closed the gates. I ordered that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. I stationed some of my young servants at the gates so that no burdens would be carried on the Sabbath day.

relationship: explicit appeal to the inherited Sabbath command
rationale: Jeremiah commands the Sabbath's consecration and cessation from work, identifying this as what God commanded the fathers. Exodus supplies the command to keep the Sabbath holy and perform no work on it.
source_text: and do not bring burdens out of your houses on the Sabbath day, and you must do no work; consecrate the Sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. And they did not hear or incline their ear,

target_units.text: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
For six days you shall labour and do all your works;

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it: you, and your son, and your daughter, your male slave, and your female slave, your ox, and your beast of burden, and all your livestock, and the resident foreigner who dwells with you.

relationship: close hardened-neck refusal to hear inherited commandments
rationale: Jeremiah describes a neck hardened beyond the fathers and refusal to hear or accept instruction. The confession in Nehemiah likewise joins the fathers' stiffened necks with refusal to hear God's commandments.
source_text: and they hardened their neck beyond their fathers, so as not to hear Me or accept instruction.

target_units.text: “But they and our fathers acted arrogantly, stiffened their necks and did not listen to Thy commandments.

“They refused to listen and did not remember Thy wonders that Thou hadst done among them. They stiffened their necks and appointed leadership to return to their slavery in Egypt. But Thou art a merciful and compassionate God, longsuffering and abundant in mercy, and Thou didst not abandon them.

relationship: parallel conditional blessing attached to Sabbath observance
rationale: Jeremiah introduces blessing with the condition of listening, keeping the Sabbath holy and doing no work. Isaiah likewise conditions promised good upon honoring the Sabbath and refraining from one's own wishes and work; the promised benefits are expressed differently.
source_text: And if you truly listen to Me, says the Lord, not bringing burdens through this city’s gates on the Sabbath day and consecrating the Sabbath day by doing no work,

target_units.text: If you turn your foot away from the Sabbaths, from doing your wishes on the holy day, and call the Sabbaths delightful, holy to your God, you will not lift your foot for work or speak a word in anger from your mouth,
and you will trust in the Lord. He will bring you up to earth’s good things and feed you your father Jacob’s inheritance, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.’”

relationship: close promise of Davidic kings entering with chariots and horses
rationale: Both passages promise kings seated on David's throne entering through gates with chariots and horses if the preceding divine instruction is obeyed. Jeremiah 17 names the city's gates, while chapter 22 names the royal house's gates.
source_text: then kings and rulers sitting on David’s throne will enter through this city’s gates, mounted on their chariots and horses, they and their rulers, Judah’s men and those dwelling in Jerusalem; and this city will be inhabited for ever.

target_units.text: Because if you truly carry out this word, kings sitting upon David’s throne and riding chariots and horses will enter this house’s gates—they, their servants, and their people.

relationship: related offerings brought to the Lord's house
rationale: Jeremiah foresees worshippers from Judah and surrounding districts bringing offerings and praise into the Lord's house. Isaiah promises acceptable burnt offerings and sacrifices there for the foreigners described in its context; the groups are distinct, while the temple-and-offering connection is explicit.
source_text: And they will come from Judah’s cities, around Jerusalem, Benjamin’s land, the plain, the mountain and the south, bringing whole burnt offerings, sacrifice, incense offerings, grain offering and frankincense, bringing praise into the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: I will bring them into My holy mountain and make them rejoice in My house of prayer. Their whole burnt offerings and sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations,”

relationship: related warning and account of Jerusalem's burning
rationale: Jeremiah threatens unquenched fire consuming Jerusalem's quarters if Sabbath instructions are rejected. Chronicles records the burning of Jerusalem's citadels and the sanctuary, then relates the desolation to the land's Sabbaths and Jeremiah's word; it does not identify this individual warning as its sole referenced prediction.
source_text: And if you do not listen to Me to consecrate the Sabbath day, not lifting burdens and not entering Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath day, I will kindle fire in her gates, and it will devour Jerusalem’s quarters and not be extinguished.

target_units.text: He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.
He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,
to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.

relationship: related commands initiating pottery-based prophetic signs
rationale: God sends Jeremiah to the potter's house to hear His words; the following pottery sign begins with a command to acquire an earthenware jar and go to a specified place. The scenes use different actions and locations, while both divine instructions prepare a material sign involving pottery.
source_text: Rise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear My words.

target_units.text: Then the Lord said to me: Go and acquire a molded earthenware jar, and bring some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests.
And go out to the burial ground of the sons of their children, which is before the Charsith Gate, and read there all the words that I speak to you.

relationship: related observation of the potter at work
rationale: Jeremiah sees the potter working upon the stones. Sirach describes a potter at work turning a wheel with his feet and shaping clay with his arm; it supplies a craft parallel without equating the source's stones with an expressly named wheel.
source_text: And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was doing work upon the stones.

target_units.text: So also a potter sitting at his work and turning a wheel with his feet, who is continually anxious over his work, and whose whole labor is measured by number.
With his arm he will shape clay, and before his feet he will bend his strength. He will give his heart to completing the coating, and his wakefulness to cleaning the kiln.

relationship: related potter's authority to shape a vessel
rationale: Jeremiah observes the potter remaking a vessel that fell apart according to what pleased him. Romans invokes the potter's authority over a lump of clay to make different vessels; it does not narrate the collapse and remaking seen by Jeremiah.
source_text: And the vessel he was making fell apart in his hands, and again he made it another vessel, as pleased him to make.

target_units.text: Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

relationship: close divine shaping of a people pictured as clay
rationale: God tells Israel that they are clay in His hands like the potter's material. Isaiah's prayer likewise calls the people clay and the work of the Lord's hands, expressly addressing Him as Father.
source_text: Can I not shape you as this potter does, house of Israel? Behold, you are like the potter’s clay in My hands.

target_units.text: But now, Lord, Thou art our Father, and we are clay, all the work of Thy hands.

relationship: close divine authority to remove and destroy nations
rationale: The Lord's announced action against a nation or kingdom recalls Jeremiah's commissioning over nations and kingdoms to uproot, demolish and destroy. Chapter 18 develops the conditional response to national conduct beyond the commissioning formula.
source_text: At last I will speak concerning a nation or kingdom, to remove them and destroy,

target_units.text: Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, demolish, destroy, build and plant.

relationship: narrative counterpart to relenting when a nation turns from evil
rationale: Jeremiah states that when a nation turns from its evils God will change His mind about the planned calamity. Jonah records Nineveh's turning from evil and God's decision not to bring the calamity He had announced.
source_text: and if that nation turns from all their evils, I will change My mind concerning the evils I planned to do to them.

target_units.text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:
“Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”
God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

relationship: close divine purpose to build and plant nations
rationale: The promised rebuilding and planting of a nation or kingdom repeats the constructive part of Jeremiah's commission to nations and kingdoms. The following verse in chapter 18 makes the nation's obedience consequential for that promise.
source_text: And at last I will speak concerning a nation and kingdom, for it to be rebuilt and planted,

target_units.text: Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, demolish, destroy, build and plant.

relationship: related reversal through subsequent wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah says a nation that does evil and refuses God's voice may lose the announced good. Ezekiel likewise says a person who trusts in his righteousness but commits lawlessness will die; the comparison distinguishes the national and individual settings.
source_text: and if they do evil things before Me by not hearing My voice, I will change My mind concerning the good things I spoke of doing for them.

target_units.text: When I speak to the righteous man—this one has trusted in his righteousness, yet commits lawlessness—none of his righteous deeds will ever be remembered. In the injustice he committed, in it he will die.

relationship: close summons to correct ways and practices
rationale: Both addresses to Judah and Jerusalem call for changed ways and improved practices. Chapter 18 sets the summons against announced evils, while the temple address promises continued settlement if the correction is real.
source_text: And now say to Judah’s men and those dwelling in Jerusalem: Behold, I am shaping evils against you and devising a design against you. Let each turn from his evil way now, and make your practices better.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Correct your ways and your practices, and I will settle you in this place.
Do not put your confidence in yourselves on false words, because they will not benefit you at all when they say, ‘The Lord’s temple, the Lord’s temple it is.’
For if you truly correct your ways and practices and truly execute judgment between a man and his neighbor,

relationship: close refusal expressed as following the evil heart
rationale: Jeremiah 18 reports the people's determination to follow their turnings away and what pleases each evil heart. Jeremiah 7 likewise describes refusal to listen and following the thoughts of their evil heart.
source_text: And they said: We will be resolute, because we will follow our turnings away, and each will do what pleases his evil heart.

target_units.text: And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, but they walked in the thoughts of their evil heart and went backward rather than forward.

relationship: close appeal to the nations to expose Israel's extraordinary infidelity
rationale: Both challenge hearers to look among the nations for anything like Israel's conduct. Chapter 2 specifies exchanging their glory and heaven's astonishment; chapter 18 calls virgin Israel's actions horrifying.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask now among the nations: Who heard such horrifying things that virgin Israel committed so greatly?

target_units.text: Cross over to the islands of Kittim and see; send to Kedar and consider carefully. See whether such things have happened.
Will nations exchange their gods, though these are not gods? But My people exchanged their glory, from which they will not benefit.
Heaven was astonished at this and shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord.

relationship: related abandonment of the ancient paths
rationale: Jeremiah 18 combines forgotten allegiance with weakening in age-old tracks and stepping onto paths unfit for travel. Jeremiah 6 urges seeking the Lord's eternal paths and walking the good way, followed by the people's refusal.
source_text: Because My people forgot Me, they burned incense in vain; and they will become weak in their ways, the age-old tracks, to step upon paths having no road for travel,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the roads and see, and ask for the Lord’s eternal paths and see which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find purification for your souls. And they said, ‘We will not go.’

relationship: close astonishment and hissing over a devastated place
rationale: Jeremiah predicts a ruined land that makes passersby astonished and shake their heads. The warning to Solomon similarly predicts astonishment and hissing at the Lord's house, explaining the calamity by abandonment of God.
source_text: to make their land a ruin and an eternal hissing; all who pass through it will be astonished and shake their head.

target_units.text: As for this lofty house, everyone passing through it will be astonished and hiss, saying, ‘Why has the Lord done this to this land and this house?’

They will say, ‘Because they abandoned the Lord their God, who brought their fathers out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, took hold of foreign gods, bowed down to them, and served them; therefore the Lord brought this calamity upon them.’”

relationship: related divine scattering expressed through wind imagery
rationale: Jeremiah compares the people's scattering before enemies to a scorching wind. Ezekiel says God will scatter a portion of Jerusalem's people to every wind; the passages share divine dispersion without making the winds' descriptions identical.
source_text: Like a scorching wind I will scatter them before their enemies; I will show them their day of destruction.

target_units.text: A quarter of you will be consumed by death; a quarter of you will perish by famine within you; a quarter of you I will scatter to every wind; and a quarter of you will fall by the sword around you, and I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: close conspiracy using the tongue as a weapon
rationale: Jeremiah's opponents devise a plan and propose striking him with the tongue. The psalm describes an evildoers' conspiracy whose sharpened tongues are like a sword and who discuss concealed traps; it does not support reversing Jeremiah's final statement that they will hear his words.
source_text: And they said: Come, let us devise a design against Jeremiah, because law will not perish from a priest, counsel from the discerning, or word from a prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and we will hear all his words.

target_units.text: Thou didst shelter me from a conspiracy of evildoers, from a multitude working lawlessness,
who sharpened their tongues like a sword and stretched their bow—a bitter deed—
to shoot down a blameless one in hidden places; suddenly they will shoot him down and will not fear.
They strengthened an evil word for themselves; they discussed concealing traps; they said, “Who will see them?”

relationship: close plea that God hear the speaker's claim of right
rationale: Jeremiah asks the Lord to attend to the voice of his claim of right. The psalm similarly asks the Lord to hear righteousness and petition and to issue judgment from His presence.
source_text: Listen to me, Lord, and listen to the voice of my claim of right.

target_units.text: A prayer of David. Hear my righteousness, Lord; attend to my petition; give ear to my prayer, not from deceitful lips.
May my judgment come forth from Thy presence; let my eyes see upright things.

relationship: close lament over evil repaid for good
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether evil should repay good and recalls interceding for his opponents. The psalm likewise laments repayment of evil for good and describes prayer, fasting and concern for those who troubled the speaker.
source_text: Is evil repaid for good things? For they spoke words together against my soul and hid their punishment for me. Remember my standing before Thee to speak good things for them, to turn Thy fury from them.

target_units.text: They repaid me evils for good things, and childlessness to my soul.
But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer will return to my bosom.
As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I sought to please; like one mourning and downcast, so I humbled myself.

relationship: parallel imprecation involving widows and bereaved children
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the attackers' families suffer widowhood, childlessness and death. The psalm's imprecation likewise asks widowhood, orphanhood and destruction of children; the parallel concerns the petitions' content, not a general instruction to inflict these harms.
source_text: Therefore give their sons to famine and gather them into the sword’s hands. Let their women become childless and widowed, their men killed by death, and their young men fallen by the sword in war.

target_units.text: Let his sons become orphans and his wife a widow.
Let his sons be shaken and migrate, and let them beg; let them be cast out from their house sites.
Let a lender search out everything he possesses; let strangers plunder his toils.
Let no helper exist for him, nor anyone compassionate toward his orphans.
Let his children be destroyed; in one generation let his name be erased.

relationship: related judgment upon those concealing traps
rationale: Jeremiah asks for a cry in their houses and anticipates sudden robbers upon people who planned his capture and hid traps. The psalm describes an unjustly concealed trap and asks that the hidden snare catch those who set it.
source_text: Let there be a cry in their houses; Thou wilt bring robbers upon them suddenly, because they attempted a plan for my capture and hid traps against me.

target_units.text: For without cause they hid for me the destruction of their trap; without purpose they reproached my soul.
Let a trap they do not know come upon them; let the snare they hid catch them, and into that trap they will fall.

relationship: parallel imprecation that sin remain before the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the opponents' injustices not be acquitted or their sins erased from before God. The psalm likewise asks that family lawlessness and sin remain remembered before the Lord rather than erased.
source_text: And Thou, Lord, knewest all their counsel against me for death. Do not acquit their injustices or erase their sins from before Thee. Let their weakness be before Thee; act among them in the time of Thy fury.

target_units.text: May his fathers’ lawlessness be remembered before the Lord, and may his mother’s sin not be erased.
Let them be before the Lord continually, and may their memorial be destroyed from the earth,

relationship: related material signs announcing Jerusalem's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to obtain an earthenware jar, which the following oracle will use to depict the city's destruction. Ezekiel is commanded to take a brick, draw Jerusalem upon it and enact a siege, explicitly calling this a sign; the objects and enacted actions differ.
source_text: Then the Lord said to me: Go and acquire a molded earthenware jar, and bring some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, take a brick, set it before your face, and draw upon it a city—Jerusalem;
lay siege to it, build forward defenses against it, throw up a palisade against it, set camps against it, and arrange missile positions all around.
Take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between you and the city. Prepare your face against it; it will be besieged, and you will besiege it. This is a sign for the sons of Israel.

relationship: related prophetic judgment at the Hinnom burial site
rationale: Jeremiah is directed to the burial ground for the proclamation whose later verse names the Son of Hinnom. The earlier oracle likewise names Hinnom and announces that the place associated with burning children will become a burial place of the slain; the Charsith Gate is named only here.
source_text: And go out to the burial ground of the sons of their children, which is before the Charsith Gate, and read there all the words that I speak to you.

target_units.text: And they built Topheth’s altar, which is in the ravine of the son of Hinnom, to burn up their sons and daughters in fire, which I did not command them and did not conceive in My heart.

Therefore behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they will no longer say Topheth’s Altar or Ravine of the Son of Hinnom, but Ravine of the Slain; and they will bury in Topheth because there is no space.

relationship: close announcement that both ears will ring at divine judgment
rationale: Both divine announcements say the coming action will make both ears of everyone hearing it ring or resound. The judgments concern different settings: Judah and Jerusalem here, and Eli's house in Samuel's surrounding oracle.
source_text: And say to them: Hear the Lord’s word, kings of Judah, men of Judah, inhabitants of Jerusalem, and those entering these gates. Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Behold, I am bringing evils upon this place, so that both ears of everyone hearing them will ring.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Samuel, “Behold, I am carrying out My words in Israel, so that both ears of everyone who hears them will resound.

relationship: close warning of ear-ringing calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah
rationale: The warning in Kings explicitly names Jerusalem and Judah and says both ears of everyone hearing will ring. It supplies a particularly close counterpart to this announcement, beyond the earlier expression in Samuel concerning another household.
source_text: And say to them: Hear the Lord’s word, kings of Judah, men of Judah, inhabitants of Jerusalem, and those entering these gates. Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Behold, I am bringing evils upon this place, so that both ears of everyone hearing them will ring.

target_units.text: not so! Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Behold, I am bringing disasters upon Jerusalem and Judah, so that both ears of everyone hearing shall ring.

relationship: historical counterpart to filling Jerusalem with innocent blood
rationale: Jeremiah accuses Judah's kings of filling the place with innocent blood. Kings specifically recounts Manasseh's pouring out innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from end to end, alongside his leading Judah into sin.
source_text: Because they abandoned Me and alienated this place, burning incense in it to foreign gods whom neither they nor their fathers knew; and Judah’s kings filled this place with innocent blood,

target_units.text: Manasseh also poured out very much innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem from end to end, besides his sins by which he caused Judah to do evil in the Lord’s eyes.

relationship: close rejection of child-burning never commanded by God
rationale: Both condemn burning children and expressly deny that God commanded or conceived it in His heart. Chapter 19 names Baal's high places, while chapter 7 identifies Topheth's altar in the Hinnom ravine.
source_text: and built high places for Baal to burn their sons in fire, things I did not command or speak of or conceive in My heart.

target_units.text: And they built Topheth’s altar, which is in the ravine of the son of Hinnom, to burn up their sons and daughters in fire, which I did not command them and did not conceive in My heart.

relationship: close renaming of Hinnom as a place of slaughter
rationale: Both announce coming days when the former name associated with Hinnom will give way to a name identifying the slaughtered. The supplied names differ in wording: Burial Ground of Slaughter here and Ravine of the Slain in chapter 7.
source_text: Therefore behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and this place will no longer be called Collapse or the Burial Ground of the Son of Hinnom, but the Burial Ground of Slaughter.

target_units.text: Therefore behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they will no longer say Topheth’s Altar or Ravine of the Son of Hinnom, but Ravine of the Slain; and they will bury in Topheth because there is no space.

relationship: close judgment of corpses becoming food for birds and beasts
rationale: Both predict that the people's dead will feed the birds of heaven and beasts of the earth. Chapter 19 places this after military defeat and the collapse of Judah's and Jerusalem's counsel.
source_text: And I will slaughter Judah’s counsel and Jerusalem’s counsel in this place, and cast them down by the sword before their enemies and into the hands of those seeking their lives. I will give their dead as food to the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the earth.

target_units.text: And this people’s dead will be food for heaven’s birds and the earth’s wild beasts, and there will be no one to drive them off.

relationship: close desolation and dismayed passersby
rationale: Both portray a devastated place drawing a dismayed response from everyone passing through. Chapter 19 specifies the city and its wound; chapter 18 speaks of the land, astonishment and shaking heads.
source_text: And I will make this city a ruin and a hissing. Everyone passing through it will look gloomy and hiss over its whole wound.

target_units.text: to make their land a ruin and an eternal hissing; all who pass through it will be astonished and shake their head.

relationship: close siege calamity of eating one's children
rationale: Jeremiah's prediction that besieged people will eat their sons and daughters directly parallels the covenant warning about consuming children under enemy-imposed distress. Jeremiah additionally names the flesh of one's neighbor.
source_text: And they will eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and each will eat his neighbor’s flesh in the encirclement and siege with which their enemies will besiege them.

target_units.text: And you shall eat the offspring of your womb, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters whom the Lord your God has given you, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemy shall afflict you.
The tender and most delicate man among you shall look grudgingly upon his brother, and the wife of his bosom, and the children who remain unto him,
begrudging any of them the flesh of his children which he eats, because nothing is left unto him, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemies shall afflict you in all your cities.

And the tender and most delicate woman among you, whose foot has never ventured to tread upon the earth because of her delicacy and tenderness, shall look grudgingly upon the husband of her bosom, and her son, and her daughter,

and upon her afterbirth which comes forth from between her thighs, and the child whom she bears; for she shall eat them secretly for want of all things, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemy shall afflict you in all your cities.

relationship: lamented counterpart to children becoming food during calamity
rationale: Jeremiah announces children being eaten during siege. Lamentations describes famine and compassionate women boiling their children as food at the people's shattering, providing a retrospective lament alongside the covenant warning.
source_text: And they will eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and each will eat his neighbor’s flesh in the encirclement and siege with which their enemies will besiege them.

target_units.text: Those wounded by the sword were better off than those wounded by famine; they went away pierced through, deprived of the fields’ produce.
The hands of compassionate women boiled their children; they became food for them at the shattering of the daughter of my people.

relationship: related breaking of pottery as an image of judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to smash the jar publicly, and the next verse interprets the act as judgment on the people and city. The psalm likewise pictures the crushing of nations as a potter's vessel; it does not depict Jeremiah's enacted sign.
source_text: And smash the jar before the eyes of the men going out with you,

target_units.text: You will shepherd them with an iron rod; you will crush them like a potter’s vessel.’”

relationship: close image of irreparable destruction through shattered earthenware
rationale: Jeremiah explains that people and city will be smashed like a vessel that cannot be healed again. Isaiah similarly compares judgment to an earthen vessel broken into pieces too small for useful recovery.
source_text: and say: Thus says the Lord: This is how I will smash this people and this city, as an earthenware vessel is smashed that cannot be healed again.

target_units.text: and its fall will be like the shattering of an earthen vessel, fine pieces from a jar, so that no shard is found among them with which to lift fire or draw a little water.”

relationship: close condemnation of rooftop worship of heaven's host
rationale: Jeremiah identifies houses where incense was burned on rooftops to heaven's host and drink offerings were poured to foreign gods. Zephaniah's judgment upon Judah and Jerusalem likewise singles out people worshipping heaven's army on rooftops.
source_text: And Jerusalem’s houses and the houses of Judah’s kings will be like the collapsing place of uncleannesses, in all the houses where they burned incense upon their roofs to all the host of the heavens and poured drink offerings to foreign gods.

target_units.text: I will stretch My hand against Judah and all Jerusalem’s inhabitants, and remove from this place the names of Baal and the names of the priests,
those worshiping the army of heaven on rooftops, those swearing by the Lord and those swearing by their king,

relationship: close prophetic proclamation in the temple courtyard
rationale: Jeremiah stands in the courtyard of the Lord's house to speak to the people after the pottery sign. The oracle in chapter 33 explicitly commands him to stand in that courtyard and deliver the Lord's words to Judeans coming to worship.
source_text: And Jeremiah came from Collapse, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, stood in the courtyard of the Lord’s house, and said to all the people:

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Stand in the courtyard of the Lord’s house and deliver an oracle to all the Judeans and all who come to bow down in the Lord’s house—all the words I commanded you to deliver to them. Do not take away a word.

relationship: close hardened-neck refusal to hear God's words
rationale: Both connect stubbornly hardened necks with refusal to hear the divine message. Chapter 19 announces the threatened evils upon the city and its dependent settlements as the consequence.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing upon this city, all its towns, and its villages all the evils I spoke against it, because they hardened their necks so as not to listen to My words.

target_units.text: And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, and they hardened their neck beyond their fathers.

relationship: related beating and physical confinement of proclaimed messengers
rationale: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and places him in a trap after hearing his prophecy. Acts records Paul and Silas beaten and placed in prison with their feet in stocks; the authorities, setting and named restraint differ.
source_text: And he struck him and put him into the trap, which was at the gate of the separated upper house that was in the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: The crowd joined the attack against them. The magistrates tore off their garments and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to keep them securely.
Having received such an order, he put them in the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.

relationship: related warning and account of Judah's defeat and Babylonian captivity
rationale: Jeremiah announces death by enemy swords and deportation of Judah into Babylon's king's hands. Chronicles recounts the Chaldean king's killings and deportation of survivors to Babylon; it does not identify the fate of every friend of Pashhur.
source_text: Because thus says the Lord: Behold, I am giving you to migration with all your friends. They will fall by their enemies’ sword, and your eyes will see. I will give you and all Judah into the hands of Babylon’s king, and they will deport them and cut them down with swords.

target_units.text: He brought against them a king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary and did not spare Zedekiah. They had no mercy on their virgins and carried away their elders. He handed everything into their hands.
All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, the treasures, and all the treasures of the king and the magnates—he brought everything into Babylon.
He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.
He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,

relationship: close transfer of royal treasures to Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah announces that the city's strength, labors and royal treasures will be carried to Babylon. Chronicles records the transfer of temple vessels and treasures of the king and magnates there, supplying a concrete historical counterpart to the treasure clause.
source_text: And I will give all this city’s strength, all its labors, and all the treasures of Judah’s king into his enemies’ hands, and they will bring them to Babylon.

target_units.text: All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, the treasures, and all the treasures of the king and the magnates—he brought everything into Babylon.

relationship: related Babylonian doom associated with unauthorized prophecy
rationale: Pashhur and those to whom he prophesied falsehood are told they will die in Babylon. The later oracle names Ahab and Zedekiah as condemned through Babylon's king and links their fate with an oracle God did not command; the condemned people and manner of death differ.
source_text: And you and all who dwell in your house will go into captivity. In Babylon you will die and there be buried—you and all your friends to whom you prophesied false things.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord concerning Ahab and Zedekiah: Behold, I am giving them into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will strike them before your eyes.
And all Judah’s deportees in Babylon will take a curse from them, saying: May the Lord make you as He made Zedekiah and Ahab, whom Babylon’s king fried in fire,

because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel: they committed adultery with their fellow citizens’ wives and delivered an oracle in My name that I did not command them. I am a witness, says the Lord.

relationship: related reproach endured in relation to God
rationale: Jeremiah addresses the Lord about being overpowered and becoming a continually mocked laughingstock. The psalm describes reproach endured on God's account and public mockery; it does not reproduce Jeremiah's charge that God deceived him.
source_text: Thou didst deceive me, Lord, and I was deceived. Thou tookest hold and didst prevail. I became a laughingstock; all day I continued being mocked.

target_units.text: for on Thine account I endured reproach; embarrassment covered my face.
I became estranged from my brothers and a foreigner to my mother’s sons,
for zeal for Thy house devoured me, and the reproaches of those reproaching Thee fell upon me.
I bowed my soul down in fasting, and it became a reproach to me.
I made sackcloth my garment, and became a proverb to them.
Those sitting in the gate talked against me, and wine-drinkers sang about me.

relationship: related reproach incurred through association with God
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord's word became reproach and derision to him. The psalm says reproaches directed at God fell upon the speaker; this comparison concerns transferred reproach and does not paraphrase Jeremiah's unusual opening as a cry against violence.
source_text: Because I will laugh with my bitter word; I will call upon rejection and misery, because the Lord’s word became a reproach and a derision to me all day long.

target_units.text: for zeal for Thy house devoured me, and the reproaches of those reproaching Thee fell upon me.

relationship: related inability to withhold prophecy after divine speech
rationale: Jeremiah describes his failed resolve to stop speaking in the Lord's name. Amos asks who will not prophesy when the Lord has spoken, expressing the compelling force of divine speech without Jeremiah's bodily fire image.
source_text: And I said: I will certainly not name the Lord’s name or speak in His name again. And it became like a burning fire blazing in my bones; I am weakened on every side and cannot bear it.

target_units.text: A lion will roar—and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—and who will not prophesy?

relationship: close movement from attempted silence to inward fire and speech
rationale: Jeremiah's attempted silence becomes unbearable burning in his bones. The psalm moves from guarding the mouth and remaining silent to a hot heart, kindled fire and speech; its stated concern about avoiding sin differs from Jeremiah's resolve to abandon prophecy.
source_text: And I said: I will certainly not name the Lord’s name or speak in His name again. And it became like a burning fire blazing in my bones; I am weakened on every side and cannot bear it.

target_units.text: I said, “I will guard my ways so as not to sin with my tongue.” I placed a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me.
I became mute and was humbled and kept silent from good things, and my pain was renewed.
My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will be kindled. I spoke with my tongue:

relationship: close report of surrounding reproach and conspiracy against the speaker
rationale: Both speakers hear the reproach of many around them and describe people gathering or acting together against them. Jeremiah additionally records supposed friends watching for deception so they may take revenge.
source_text: Because I heard the reproach of many gathering all around: Rise against him, and let us rise against him, all you men who are his friends! Watch his purpose, to see whether he will be deceived and we can prevail against him and take our revenge on him.

target_units.text: For I heard the reproach of many dwelling all around; as they gathered together against me, they planned to take my soul.

relationship: parallel divine combat on behalf of a threatened speaker
rationale: Jeremiah declares that the Lord is with him like a strong fighter. The psalm petitions the Lord to make war on the speaker's attackers, take weapons and block his pursuers; one declares confidence while the other asks for such intervention.
source_text: And the Lord is with me like a strong fighter. Therefore they pursued and could not understand; they were greatly shamed, because they did not understand their dishonors, which will never be forgotten.

target_units.text: Of David. Judge, Lord, those who wrong me; make war on those who make war on me.
Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise to my aid.
Draw the sword and close the way against those pursuing me; say to my soul, “I am your salvation.”

relationship: close appeal to God's inward knowledge for vindication
rationale: Both appeals ask to see God's vengeance upon opponents because the speaker disclosed his defense or claim of right to Him. Jeremiah 20 says God understands kidneys and hearts, while chapter 11 says He tests them; the appeals preserve that verbal distinction within their close correspondence.
source_text: Lord, testing righteous things, understanding kidneys and hearts: May I see the vengeance from Thee among them, because to Thee I disclosed my defenses.

target_units.text: Lord, who judges justly, who tests kidneys and hearts, may I see the vengeance from Thee upon them, because to Thee I revealed my claim of right.

relationship: close praise for rescue of the poor from hostile hands
rationale: Jeremiah commands praise because the Lord rescued a poor person's life from evildoers' hands. The psalm celebrates the Lord's rescue of the poor and needy from stronger people and plunderers.
source_text: Sing to the Lord; praise Him, because He rescued a poor person’s life from the hand of those doing evil.

target_units.text: All my bones will say, “Lord, who is like Thee, rescuing the poor from the hand of those stronger than he is, and the poor and needy from those plundering him?”

relationship: close curse upon the day of one's birth
rationale: Jeremiah curses the day his mother bore him. Job likewise curses his day and wishes the day of his birth to perish and become dark, expressing a closely related birth lament.
source_text: Accursed be the day on which I was born! Let the day my mother bore me not be a day to pray for!

target_units.text: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day,
saying:
“May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which they said, ‘Behold, a male child!’
May that day be darkness; may the Lord above not seek it out, and may no brightness come upon it.

relationship: related reversal of the announcement of a male child's birth
rationale: Jeremiah curses the man who joyfully announced a boy's birth to his father. Job curses the night in which a male child was announced; the target of the curse is the time in Job, not the announcing person.
source_text: Accursed be the man who brought my father good news, saying, A boy has been born to you!—rejoicing.

target_units.text: “May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which they said, ‘Behold, a male child!’

relationship: related comparison with cities overthrown by the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah wishes the birth-announcer to become like cities God overthrew in fury. Genesis supplies the explicit account of the Lord overthrowing Sodom and Gomorrah; Jeremiah's individual verse leaves the cities unnamed.
source_text: Let that man be like the cities the Lord overthrew in fury without changing His mind. Let him hear a cry in the morning and a battle shout at noon,

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: close wish that life had ended in the womb
rationale: Jeremiah wishes he had been killed in his mother's womb so that it became his tomb. Job asks why he did not die in the womb and compares the wished-for fate to miscarriage or infants who never saw light; Jeremiah's everlasting-conception image is distinctive.
source_text: because he did not kill me in my mother’s womb, so that my mother would have become my tomb and the womb one of everlasting conception.

target_units.text: because it did not close the gates of my mother’s womb; for it would have removed pain from my eyes.
For why did I not die in the womb, come out from the belly and immediately perish?
Why did knees meet me? Why did I suck breasts?
Now I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept and rested
with kings, counselors of the earth, who exulted in swords,
or with rulers who had much gold, who filled their houses with silver,
or like a miscarriage coming out of a mother’s womb, or like infants who never saw light.

relationship: parallel question about life given for suffering
rationale: Jeremiah asks why he emerged from the womb to experience labor, pain and shame. Job asks why light and life are given to people in bitterness and pain who long for death.
source_text: Why did I come out from the womb to see labors and pains, and have my days continue in shame?

target_units.text: For why has light been given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain,
who long for death and do not obtain it, digging for it as for treasures,
and become overjoyed if they obtain it?
Death is rest for a man, for God has shut him in.

relationship: close account of Zedekiah sending Zephaniah to Jeremiah
rationale: Both reports name King Zedekiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah in a delegation to Jeremiah. The other messenger differs: Pashhur here and Jehucal in chapter 44.
source_text: The word that came from the Lord to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:

target_units.text: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest to Jeremiah, saying, Please pray for us to the Lord.

relationship: related royal inquiry about relief from the Babylonian siege
rationale: Zedekiah's delegation asks whether divine wonders will make Babylon's king withdraw. The later reply to a king who sent to seek the Lord rules out lasting Chaldean withdrawal and announces the city's burning.
source_text: Ask the Lord about us, because Babylon’s king has come against us, whether the Lord will act according to all His wonders, so that he goes away from us.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Tell Judah’s king, who sent to you to seek Me, Pharaoh’s force, which came out to help you, will return to Egypt’s land.
The Chaldeans themselves will return, fight this city, seize it, and burn it with fire.
For thus said the Lord: Do not suppose within yourselves, The Chaldeans will flee and leave us. They certainly will not leave.
Even if you struck the whole Chaldean force fighting you and some were left pierced through, each in his place, these would rise and burn this city with fire.

relationship: related futility of armed resistance to the announced capture
rationale: Jeremiah 21 announces the turning of Judah's weapons into the besieged city. Chapter 44 says even surviving wounded Chaldeans would rise to burn the city; both undermine military confidence without describing identical actions upon the weapons.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am turning the weapons of war with which you fight the Chaldeans who have shut you in outside the wall into this city,

target_units.text: Even if you struck the whole Chaldean force fighting you and some were left pierced through, each in his place, these would rise and burn this city with fire.

relationship: close declaration that God Himself fights His disobedient people
rationale: Jeremiah says God Himself will fight the city with anger and might. Isaiah recalls the people's disobedience and says God turned hostile and Himself fought them, reversing the preceding account of His saving action.
source_text: and I Myself will fight you with outstretched hand and mighty arm, with fury, anger, and great indignation.

target_units.text: But they disobeyed and provoked His holy spirit. He turned toward hostility against them and Himself fought them.

relationship: close divine judgment by death upon people and livestock
rationale: Jeremiah announces a great death striking the city's human and animal inhabitants. Ezekiel similarly describes God sending death upon a land in wrath to destroy human beings and livestock.
source_text: And I will strike all this city’s inhabitants, the people and the livestock, with a great death, and they will die.

target_units.text: Or even if I send death upon that land and pour My wrath upon it in blood, to destroy human and livestock from it,

relationship: related unspared judgment through death, famine and sword
rationale: Jeremiah names survivors of death, famine and sword being handed to enemies without divine sparing. Ezekiel's Jerusalem oracle likewise denies sparing and names death, famine and sword, while apportioning its judgments differently.
source_text: And afterward—thus says the Lord—I will give Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants, and the people remaining in this city after death, famine, and sword into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives. They will cut them down with the sword’s edge. I will not spare them or have compassion on them.

target_units.text: Therefore, as I live, says the Lord, surely, because you defiled My holy places with all your abominations, I too will reject you. My eye will not spare, and I too will have no mercy.

A quarter of you will be consumed by death; a quarter of you will perish by famine within you; a quarter of you I will scatter to every wind; and a quarter of you will fall by the sword around you, and I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: close setting of life and death before the hearers
rationale: Both addresses explicitly set life and death before their audience. Deuteronomy frames the choice through covenant obedience; Jeremiah immediately applies it to remaining in the city or going out to the Chaldeans.
source_text: And say to this people: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death.

target_units.text: Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His ordinances and His judgments, then you shall live and be many; and the Lord your God shall bless you in all the land into which you go to inherit it.
And if your heart turns aside, and you will not hearken, and you are led astray to bow down unto other gods and serve them,
I declare unto you this day that you shall surely perish, and you shall in no wise be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you, into which you are crossing the Jordan to inherit it.
I call heaven and earth to witness unto you this day: I have set before your face life and death, the blessing and the curse. Choose life, that you and your seed may live,

relationship: close repeated promise of life through going out to the Chaldeans
rationale: Both announcements contrast death by sword and famine for those staying in the city with life for those going out to the Chaldeans. The life described as spoil here is called gain in chapter 45.
source_text: Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine; whoever goes out to join the Chaldeans who have shut you in will live, and his life will be spoil, and he will live.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Whoever remains in this city will die by sword and famine. Whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live; his life will be his gain, and he will live.

relationship: close prediction of capture and burning by Babylon's king
rationale: Both announce that the city will be handed over to Babylon's king and burned with fire. Jeremiah 21 expressly states God's intention of evils rather than good for the city.
source_text: Because I have fixed My face upon this city for evils and not for good things. It will be handed into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will burn it down with fire.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord: Go to Zedekiah king of Judah and tell him, Thus said the Lord: This city will certainly be handed over to Babylon’s king. He will seize it and burn it with fire.

relationship: close summons to Judah's royal house to hear
rationale: The brief address to the house of Judah's king is expanded in chapter 22's address to the king seated on David's throne, his household and people. Both introduce instructions about royal justice, not merely an unrelated prophetic speech formula.
source_text: House of Judah’s king, hear the Lord’s word.

target_units.text: and say: Hear the Lord’s word, king of Judah who sits on David’s throne—you, your household, your people, and those entering these gates.

relationship: parallel royal duty to judge justly and rescue the vulnerable
rationale: The house of David is commanded to set judgment straight and rescue the plundered. The psalm for Solomon asks righteous royal judgment and describes the king saving the children of the needy and humbling the false accuser.
source_text: House of David, thus says the Lord: Judge a judgment in the morning, set things straight, and rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him, so that My anger is not kindled like fire and burns with no one to quench it.

target_units.text: For Solomon. God, give Thy judgment to the king, and Thy righteousness to the king’s son,
to judge Thy people in righteousness, and Thy poor in justice.
Let the mountains take up peace for Thy people, and the hills in righteousness.
He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the needy, and humble the false accuser,

relationship: related proud confidence that a dwelling cannot be overcome
rationale: Jeremiah confronts inhabitants who ask who could frighten them or enter their dwelling. Obadiah confronts Idumea's confidence in a lofty dwelling with God's promise to bring it down; the source's valley setting is distinct from Obadiah's height imagery.
source_text: Behold, I am against you who dwell in the valley of Sor, the level land, you who say, Who will frighten us? Or who will enter our dwelling?

target_units.text: The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who camp in holes in the rocks, raising his dwelling high and saying in his heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”
If you soar like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.

relationship: related divine judgment pictured as consuming woodland fire
rationale: Jeremiah announces fire consuming the city's woodland and everything around it. Isaiah likewise describes a divinely sent burning that consumes woodland, forests and more, in its surrounding judgment upon arrogant power.
source_text: And I will kindle a fire in her woodland, and it will consume everything around her.

target_units.text: And it will not be so; rather, the Lord Sabaoth will send dishonor against your honor, and against your glory a burning fire will burn.
Israel’s light will become fire, and He will sanctify him in burning fire and consume the woodland like grass. On that day,
the mountains, hills and forests will be extinguished, and it will consume from soul to flesh. The one fleeing will be like someone fleeing from a burning flame.

relationship: close summons to Judah's ruler and gate-entering people
rationale: Both call Judah's ruler or rulers and the gate-entering people to hear the Lord's word. Chapter 22 places the royal summons within an instruction on justice, whereas chapter 17 proceeds to Sabbath observance.
source_text: and say: Hear the Lord’s word, king of Judah who sits on David’s throne—you, your household, your people, and those entering these gates.

target_units.text: and you will say to them: Hear the Lord’s word, kings of Judah, all Judea and all Jerusalem, who enter these gates:

relationship: close protection of the newcomer, widow and orphan
rationale: Jeremiah commands the royal audience not to oppress the newcomer, orphan or widow. Exodus explicitly forbids mistreating the resident foreigner and widow or orphan, warning that God hears their distress.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Do justice and righteousness; rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him. Do not oppress the newcomer, orphan, or widow, and do not act impiously or shed innocent blood in this place.

target_units.text: And you shall not ill-treat a resident foreigner, neither shall you afflict him; for you were resident foreigners in the land of Egypt.
You shall not mistreat any widow or orphan.
But if you afflict them, and they cry aloud to Me, I will surely listen to their voice,
I will be angry with wrath and kill you with the sword. Your wives will become widows and your children orphans.

relationship: parallel conditional continuance of the Davidic throne
rationale: Jeremiah promises kings seated on David's throne entering the royal house if the preceding word is carried out. God's address to Solomon likewise conditions the establishment of his royal throne upon faithful conduct and obedience.
source_text: Because if you truly carry out this word, kings sitting upon David’s throne and riding chariots and horses will enter this house’s gates—they, their servants, and their people.

target_units.text: As for you, if you walk before Me as your father David walked, with holiness of heart and uprightness, doing all I commanded him, and keep My ordinances and commandments,
then I will establish your royal throne over Israel for ever, as I told your father David, saying, ‘A man ruling in Israel shall not be removed from you.’

relationship: parallel warning that disobedience brings desolation upon a house
rationale: Jeremiah warns that refusal of God's words will make the royal house desolate. The warning to Solomon says turning away will lead to the consecrated temple's rejection and public astonishment; the royal house and sanctuary must not be conflated.
source_text: But if you do not carry out these words, I swear by Myself, says the Lord, that this house will become a desolation.

target_units.text: But if you and your children indeed turn away from Me and do not keep My commandments and ordinances which Moses set before you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them,

then I will remove Israel from the land I gave them and cast away from My presence this house I consecrated for My name. Israel shall become a disappearance and a subject of talk among all the peoples.
As for this lofty house, everyone passing through it will be astonished and hiss, saying, ‘Why has the Lord done this to this land and this house?’

relationship: related Lebanon-and-cedar imagery for Judah's royal establishment
rationale: Jeremiah addresses Judah's royal house as the head of Lebanon before announcing devastation. Ezekiel pictures an eagle taking Lebanon's cedar growth, then explicitly interprets the action as Babylon's removal of Jerusalem's king and rulers in verse 12.
source_text: Because thus says the Lord against the house of Judah’s king: You are Gilead to Me, the head of Lebanon; surely I will make you a wilderness, cities that will not be inhabited.

target_units.text: and say, ‘Thus says the Lord: The great eagle, with great wings and a broad span, full of talons, which has authority to enter Lebanon, took the cedar’s choice parts;
he nipped off the tips of its tender growth, carried them to the land of Canaan, and set them in a fortified city.

relationship: related downfall of lofty power through Lebanon imagery
rationale: Jeremiah announces a destroyer cutting chosen cedars and casting them into fire. Isaiah joins the humbling of lofty figures with Lebanon's fall; it names a sword rather than Jeremiah's axe and does not supply the same burning scene.
source_text: And I will bring against you a destroying man and his axe, and they will cut down your chosen cedars and cast them into the fire.

target_units.text: For behold, the Master, the Lord Sabaoth, throws the glorious ones into confusion with strength; those lofty in insolence will be shattered, and the high brought low,
and the high will fall by a sword, while Lebanon will fall with the high.

relationship: close question by nations about the reason for devastation
rationale: Jeremiah pictures nations passing through the city and asking why the Lord treated it this way. Deuteronomy similarly pictures all nations asking why the Lord acted against the land with great anger.
source_text: And nations will pass through this city, and each will say to his neighbor: Why did the Lord act this way toward this great city?

target_units.text: and all the nations shall say, Why has the Lord done thus unto this land? What does this great heat of anger mean?

relationship: close explanation of calamity through covenant abandonment and foreign worship
rationale: Both answer the preceding nations' question by naming abandonment of the Lord's covenant and service and worship of other gods. The correspondence includes both the question-and-answer setting and the specific explanation.
source_text: And they will say: Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord their God, bowed down to foreign gods, and served them.

target_units.text: And they shall say, Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers, which He made with their fathers when He brought them forth out of the land of Egypt;
and they went and served other gods, and bowed down unto them, whom they did not know, and whom He had not allotted unto them.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of mourning for the deported king
rationale: The command to weep for the one going out because he will not return is immediately grounded in the oracle about Shallum. The following verses specify his departure, death abroad and permanent loss of his homeland.
source_text: Do not weep for the dead or lament him; weep bitterly for the one going out, because he will never return or see his homeland.

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord concerning Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father Josiah and went out from this place: He will not return there again,
but in the place where I deported him, there he will die, and he will never see this land again.

relationship: genealogical counterpart for Shallum son of Josiah
rationale: Jeremiah names Shallum as Josiah's son. Chronicles lists Salloum among Josiah's sons, providing the corresponding filial identification under the supplied spelling without independently describing his deportation.
source_text: Because thus says the Lord concerning Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father Josiah and went out from this place: He will not return there again,

target_units.text: Josiah’s sons: Joanan the firstborn, Joakim the second, Sedekias the third, Salloum the fourth.

relationship: related account of a deposed son of Josiah dying abroad
rationale: Jeremiah predicts that Shallum will die where he was deported and never see the land again. Kings records the removal to Egypt and death there of Joachas, identified in its context as a son of Josiah. This comparison concerns the royal death abroad without assuming that the supplied names are identical.
source_text: but in the place where I deported him, there he will die, and he will never see this land again.

target_units.text: Pharaoh Nechao made Eliakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, king over them in place of his father Josiah and changed his name to Joakim. He took Joachas and brought him into Egypt, and he died there.

relationship: legal counterpart to the condemnation of withheld wages
rationale: Jeremiah condemns a builder who makes his neighbor work without payment. Leviticus forbids wronging or robbing the neighbor and withholding a hired worker's wages overnight.
source_text: O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! He works through his neighbor without payment and will not give him his wages.

target_units.text: You shall not wrong your neighbour, neither shall you rob; and the wages of the hired worker shall in no wise remain with you overnight until morning.

relationship: close denunciation of laborers' withheld payment
rationale: Jeremiah denounces unpaid work used to build the ruler's house. James denounces withheld harvest wages and says the workers' cries reach the Lord; the work differs, but the unjust retention of payment is explicit in both.
source_text: O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! He works through his neighbor without payment and will not give him his wages.

target_units.text: Look, the wages of the laborers who reaped your fields, withheld by you, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have entered the ears of the Lord Sabaoth.

relationship: related criticism surrounding elaborately finished private houses
rationale: Jeremiah describes airy upper rooms, cedar paneling and red ocher in the ruler's house, immediately after condemning its unjust construction. Haggai questions dwelling in houses with recessed ceilings while God's house lies waste; the criticized priorities and architectural details differ.
source_text: You built yourself a well-proportioned house, airy upper rooms set apart by windows, paneled with cedar and painted with red ocher.

target_units.text: “Is it time for you to live in your houses with recessed ceilings, while this house has been laid waste?

relationship: related royal responsibility for righteousness
rationale: Jeremiah's concluding judgment says doing judgment and good righteousness was better for the royal addressee. Proverbs says a righteous king raises a country while a lawless man tears it down; this comparison does not resolve Jeremiah's unusual opening about being provoked in Ahaz.
source_text: Will you reign because you are provoked in Ahaz your father? They will not eat or drink. It was better for you to do judgment and good righteousness.

target_units.text: A righteous king raises up a country, but a lawless man tears it down.

relationship: contrast concerning royal judgment for the poor
rationale: Jeremiah condemns failure to judge the cases of the lowly and poor as failure to know God. Proverbs presents the positive counterpart: a king who judges the poor in truth has an established throne.
source_text: They did not know; they did not judge a case for the lowly or a case for the poor. Is this not your failing to know Me? says the Lord.
