target_units.text: When a king judges the poor in truth, his throne will be established as a testimony.

relationship: close accusation against leaders joining greed with bloodshed
rationale: Jeremiah charges the royal addressee with greed, innocent blood and wrongdoing. Micah accuses leaders of distorted justice, building Zion with bloodshed and judging for gifts; both tie governing corruption to violent injustice.
source_text: Behold, neither your eyes nor your heart are good; instead they are directed toward your greed, innocent blood to shed it, wrongdoing, and murder to commit it.

target_units.text: Hear these things now, leaders of Jacob’s house and remaining ones of Israel’s house, who abhor justice and twist all straight things,
you who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices!

Her leaders judged with gifts, her priests answered for wages and her prophets divined for silver; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Calamities will certainly not come upon us.”

relationship: contrast between denied and promised royal mourning
rationale: Jehoiakim is denied mourning with the cry Alas, lord. The later oracle promises Zedekiah mourning and the cry O lord, creating an explicit contrast between the announced funerary treatment of two named kings.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!

target_units.text: You will die in peace. As they wept for your fathers who reigned before you, they will weep for you and lament you, O lord! For I have spoken the word, said the Lord.

relationship: close prediction of Jehoiakim's dishonored discarded corpse
rationale: Jeremiah 22 predicts a donkey's burial and the corpse thrown beyond Jerusalem's gate. The later oracle about Jehoiakim likewise says his carcass will be thrown out to the day's heat and night's frost.
source_text: He will be buried with a donkey’s burial; swept up, he will be thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate.

target_units.text: Therefore thus said the Lord concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He will have no one sitting on David’s throne. His carcass will be thrown out in the day’s heat and the night’s frost.

relationship: related lament over shattered or faithless lovers
rationale: Jeremiah's address calls for lament because all the lovers have been shattered. Lamentations describes Jerusalem without comfort among her lovers and with faithless friends turned enemies; it does not say those lovers themselves were shattered.
source_text: Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan and shout to the far side of the sea, because all your lovers have been shattered.

target_units.text: Weeping, she wept in the night, her tears upon her cheeks. Among all those who love her there is no one to comfort her. All her friends have dealt faithlessly with her; they have become her enemies.

relationship: close longstanding refusal to hear God's voice
rationale: Jeremiah 22 describes refusal to listen as the addressee's way from youth. Chapter 7 recalls the command to hear God's voice and a continuing refusal across generations, without making the two chronological descriptions identical.
source_text: I spoke to you in your falling away, and you said, I will not listen. This is your way from your youth: you did not hear My voice.

target_units.text: But this utterance I commanded them, saying: Hear My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people; and walk in all My ways that I command you, so that it may be well with you.
And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, but they walked in the thoughts of their evil heart and went backward rather than forward.
From the day their fathers left Egypt’s land until this day, I sent out to you all My servants the prophets by day and at dawn, and I sent them.
And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, and they hardened their neck beyond their fathers.

relationship: related judgment upon failed shepherds and their people
rationale: Jeremiah 22 announces that wind will shepherd the shepherds and that the lovers will be captive. Chapter 10 associates foolish shepherds who did not seek the Lord with scattering; it does not contain the same wind-as-shepherd figure.
source_text: Wind will shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers will go out in captivity. Then you will be ashamed and dishonored because of all who love you.

target_units.text: For the shepherds acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord; therefore all the pasture did not perceive, and they were scattered.

relationship: close birth-pang imagery for impending calamity
rationale: Jeremiah compares the coming pangs of the cedar-nesting addressee to a woman giving birth. Micah addresses Zion with the same birth-pang image and expressly connects it with leaving the city for Babylon.
source_text: You who dwell in Lebanon and nest among the cedars will groan when pangs come upon you like those of a woman giving birth.

target_units.text: And now why have you experienced calamities? Did you have no king? Has your counsel perished, that birth pains have seized you like a woman giving birth?

Labor in birth, be courageous and draw near, daughter of Zion, like a woman giving birth! For now you will go out from the city, camp in the plain and come as far as Babylon. From there He will rescue you, and from there the Lord your God will redeem you from your enemies’ hand.

relationship: contrast between removal and choice under the signet image
rationale: God says He would remove Jeconiah even if he were a signet on His right hand. Haggai promises to make Zerubbabel like a signet because God has chosen him; the named recipients and directions of the image are opposite.
source_text: As I live, says the Lord, even if Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, becomes a signet on My right hand, I will pull you off from there,

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will take you, Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, My servant, says the Lord, and make you like a signet, for I have chosen you, says the Lord Almighty.”

relationship: close threatened handover and recorded deportation of the same named king
rationale: The oracle identifies Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and announces his delivery into feared Chaldean hands. The later vision is dated after Nebuchadnezzar deported the same explicitly named Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim to Babylon, giving the royal handover a specific narrative counterpart.
source_text: and hand you into the hands of those seeking your life, those before whom you are afraid, into the hands of the Chaldeans.

target_units.text: The Lord showed me two baskets of figs lying before the Lord’s sanctuary, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, the rulers, craftsmen, prisoners, and rich people from Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon.

relationship: same-chapter parallel deaths abroad for differently named exiled kings
rationale: The oracle predicts that Jeconiah and his mother will die in the foreign land to which God casts them. The earlier oracle about Shallum likewise predicts death in the place of deportation. The kings are distinct, and the mother's fate is an additional feature of the Jeconiah oracle.
source_text: And I will cast you and your mother who bore you into a land where you were not born, and there you both will die.

target_units.text: but in the place where I deported him, there he will die, and he will never see this land again.

relationship: same-chapter parallel denial of return to an exiled king
rationale: The denial of return in the Jeconiah oracle parallels the earlier denial that Shallum will ever return or see the land again. These are separate royal oracles within the chapter, not an assumption that the kings are the same person.
source_text: But to the land for which they pray in their souls, they will certainly not return.

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord concerning Shallum son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father Josiah and went out from this place: He will not return there again,
but in the place where I deported him, there he will die, and he will never see this land again.

relationship: close dishonor among foreign lands pictured as a useless vessel
rationale: Jeremiah compares Jeconiah, cast into an unfamiliar land, to a vessel with no use. Hosea compares Israel among the nations to a useless vessel, applying the same dishonoring image to the people rather than one king.
source_text: Jeconiah was dishonored like a vessel for which there is no use, because he was cast out and thrown into a land he did not know.

target_units.text: Israel was swallowed up; now he became among the nations like a useless vessel.

relationship: related direct summons to the earth to hear
rationale: Jeremiah addresses the land twice and commands it to hear the Lord's word. Moses' song likewise addresses the earth as a hearer of his words, together with heaven; the scope and repeated wording differ.
source_text: Land, land, hear the Lord’s word:

target_units.text: Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

relationship: genealogical context for Jeconiah's offspring under the royal restriction
rationale: Jeremiah bars the named king's offspring from prospering on David's throne and ruling again in Judah. Matthew names Jechoniah at the Babylonian deportation and lists his offspring afterward; the genealogy does not itself say that those descendants resumed rule in Judah or resolve every implication of the oracle.
source_text: Record this man as an outcast, because no man from his offspring will grow great sitting on David’s throne and ruling again in Judah.

target_units.text: Josiah begot Jechoniah and his brothers at the deportation to Babylon.
After the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah begot Shealtiel; Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel;

relationship: close condemnation of shepherds whose sheep are scattered
rationale: Jeremiah addresses shepherds who scatter and destroy God's sheep. Ezekiel accuses Israel's shepherds of failing to feed, heal and seek the sheep, then describes their scattering and exposure to beasts.
source_text: O shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of My pasture!

target_units.text: “Son of man, prophesy against Israel’s shepherds. Prophesy and say to the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, surely shepherds do not feed themselves? Do shepherds not feed the sheep?
Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fattened animal, but you do not feed My sheep.
You have not strengthened the weak, restored the sick to health, bound up the broken, brought back the wandering or sought the lost. You have worn down the strong with toil.
My sheep scattered because there were no shepherds and became food for all the field’s beasts.
My sheep scattered on every mountain and upon every high hill, and scattered over the whole face of the earth. There was no one seeking them out or turning them back.

relationship: close divine judgment against negligent shepherds
rationale: Jeremiah says God will exact justice from shepherds who drove His sheep out and did not visit them. Ezekiel likewise declares God against the shepherds, requiring His sheep from their hands and removing their charge.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord to those shepherding My people: You scattered My sheep and drove them out without visiting them. Behold, I am exacting justice from you according to your evil practices.

target_units.text: thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require My sheep from their hands and turn them aside from shepherding My sheep. The shepherds will no longer feed them. I will rescue My sheep from their mouth, and they will no longer be food for them.

relationship: close gathering of scattered people into pasture
rationale: Jeremiah promises to receive the remnant from the lands of dispersion and establish them in pasture. Ezekiel likewise promises gathering from countries into Israel's land and good pasture, using the same restored-flock imagery.
source_text: And I will receive the remnant of My people from all the land where I drove them out, and establish them in their pasture; they will increase and multiply.

target_units.text: I will bring them out from the nations, gather them from the countries and bring them into their own land. I will feed them upon Israel’s mountains, in the ravines and in every dwelling place of the land.
I will feed them in good pasture, and their folds will be upon Israel’s high mountain. There they will lie down, there rest in good delight, and graze in rich pasture upon Israel’s mountains.

relationship: close promise of newly appointed faithful shepherds
rationale: God promises shepherds who will tend the restored people so they no longer fear. The earlier restoration oracle promises shepherds according to God's heart who shepherd with knowledge; its emphasis is their character and understanding.
source_text: And I will raise shepherds for them who will tend them, and they will no longer fear or be frightened, says the Lord.

target_units.text: and I will give you shepherds according to My heart, and they will shepherd you, shepherding with knowledge.

relationship: close Davidic rule characterized by righteousness and judgment
rationale: Jeremiah promises a righteous rising for David and a discerning king doing judgment and righteousness. Isaiah describes rule upon David's throne established and upheld in righteousness and judgment, with enduring peace.
source_text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up a righteous rising for David. A king will reign and understand, doing judgment and righteousness upon the earth.

target_units.text: Great is his rule, and his peace has no limit, upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to establish it and uphold it in righteousness and judgment, from now on and for ever. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things.

relationship: related Rising imagery associated with royal rule
rationale: Jeremiah announces a righteous rising for David who reigns as king. Zechariah names a man Rising who builds the Lord's house and rules on his throne; the target adds temple building and a priest at his right hand, rather than simply repeating Jeremiah's oracle.
source_text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up a righteous rising for David. A king will reign and understand, doing judgment and righteousness upon the earth.

target_units.text: and say to him: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Look, a man whose name is Rising! From beneath him he will rise, and he will build the Lord’s house.
He himself will receive excellence, sit and rule on his throne; the priest will be at his right hand, and peaceful counsel will be between both.

relationship: related restoration marked by safety for Israel
rationale: Jeremiah promises Judah's salvation and Israel's confident dwelling during the announced reign. Ezekiel promises that the restored flock will no longer be plunder and will dwell in hope without anyone terrifying them; it does not explain or replace the name Josedek.
source_text: In his days Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell confidently. This is his name, which the Lord will call him: Josedek.

target_units.text: They will no longer be plunder for the nations, and the land’s beasts certainly will no longer eat them. They will dwell in hope, and no one will terrify them.

relationship: close repeated replacement of the exodus oath formula
rationale: Both announce coming days when people will no longer invoke the Lord's life by identifying Him as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt. Their following verses replace that wording with the gathering from dispersion.
source_text: Therefore behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they will no longer say, As the Lord lives, who brought Israel’s house up from Egypt’s land,

target_units.text: Therefore behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and they will no longer say, ‘The Lord lives, who brought Israel’s sons up from Egypt’s land,’

relationship: close repeated oath celebrating return from the north and other lands
rationale: Both describe the new invocation of the living Lord through His gathering Israel from the northern land and all the regions of dispersion and restoring them to their land.
source_text: but, As the Lord lives, who gathered all Israel’s offspring from the northern land and all the countries where He drove them out, and restored them to their land.

target_units.text: but, ‘The Lord lives, who brought Israel’s house up from the northern land and all the regions where they were driven.’ And I will restore them to their land that I gave their fathers.

relationship: related bodily trembling in a prophetic response to divine majesty
rationale: Jeremiah describes a shattered heart and shaken bones before the Lord and His glory. Habakkuk's prayer describes terror and trembling entering the bones; it does not reproduce Jeremiah's comparison to a person gripped by wine.
source_text: Among the prophets my heart was shattered; within me all my bones were shaken. I became like a shattered man, like a person gripped by wine, before the Lord and the splendor of His glory.

target_units.text: I kept watch, and my belly was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips. Trembling entered my bones, and my bodily condition beneath me was troubled. I will rest on a day of affliction, to go up to the people of my sojourning.

relationship: close mourning land and dried vegetation associated with human evil
rationale: Jeremiah 23 joins the land's mourning and dried pastures with an evil course. Jeremiah 12 explicitly asks how long the earth and field's grass will suffer because of the inhabitants' evil.
source_text: Because of these things the land mourned and the wilderness pastures dried up. Their course became evil, and their strength was not so.

target_units.text: How long will the earth mourn and all the field’s grass dry up because of the evil of those dwelling in it? Livestock and birds vanished, because they said, ‘God will not see our ways.’

relationship: related corruption of both priestly and prophetic offices
rationale: Jeremiah identifies priest and prophet as defiled and says God saw their evils in His house. Micah accuses priests of answering for wages and prophets of divining for silver; its specified misconduct does not exhaust Jeremiah's broader accusation.
source_text: Because priest and prophet were defiled, and in My house I saw their evils.

target_units.text: Her leaders judged with gifts, her priests answered for wages and her prophets divined for silver; yet they relied upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Calamities will certainly not come upon us.”

relationship: close judgment pictured as a dark and slippery way
rationale: Jeremiah announces a slippery place in darkness where the condemned will trip and fall. The psalm similarly asks that the enemies' way become darkness and a slippery path, adding pursuit by the Lord's angel.
source_text: Therefore let their way become a slippery place for them in darkness, and they will be tripped and fall in it, because I will bring evils upon them in their year of visitation, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Let their way become darkness and a slippery path, with an angel of the Lord pursuing them.

relationship: historical counterpart to prophets serving Baal in Israel
rationale: Jeremiah condemns Samaria's prophets for prophesying through Baal and leading Israel astray. Elijah's confrontation explicitly contrasts following the Lord with following Baal and names Baal's many prophets; it does not identify every prophet in Jeremiah's accusation individually.
source_text: And among Samaria’s prophets I saw lawless acts: they prophesied through Baal and led My people Israel astray.

target_units.text: Elijah came near them all and said to them, “How long will you limp on both your knees? If the Lord is God, follow Him; if Baal is, follow him.” The people did not answer a word.
Elijah said to the people, “I remain as the Lord’s prophet utterly alone, but Baal’s prophets are four hundred fifty men, and the grove’s prophets are four hundred.

relationship: close accusation of strengthening evildoers against repentance
rationale: Jeremiah says Jerusalem's prophets support evil hands so no one turns from his evil way. Ezekiel likewise accuses the prophetic women of strengthening the lawless person's hands so he does not turn from evil and live.
source_text: And among Jerusalem’s prophets I have seen horrifying things: committing adultery, walking in lies, and supporting evil hands so that no one turns from his evil way. They all became like Sodom to Me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.

target_units.text: Because you distorted the righteous person’s heart unjustly, though I was not distorting him, and strengthened the lawless person’s hands so that he does not turn at all from his evil way and live,

relationship: related application of Sodom and Gomorrah to Judah's corrupt people
rationale: Jeremiah compares the prophets and Jerusalem's inhabitants to Sodom and Gomorrah. Isaiah's address against Judah and Jerusalem likewise invokes those cities and directly addresses rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah; the immediate groups and surrounding accusations differ.
source_text: And among Jerusalem’s prophets I have seen horrifying things: committing adultery, walking in lies, and supporting evil hands so that no one turns from his evil way. They all became like Sodom to Me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.

target_units.text: If the Lord Sabaoth had not left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.
Hear the Lord’s word, rulers of Sodom! Attend to God’s law, people of Gomorrah!

relationship: close judgment pictured as painful food and bitter drink
rationale: Jeremiah 23 threatens the prophets with pain to eat and bitter water to drink. The earlier oracle threatens the law-abandoning people with distresses as food and gall-water as drink, repeating the paired punitive nourishment image.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will feed them pain and give them bitter water to drink, because from Jerusalem’s prophets defilement went out into all the land.

target_units.text: therefore thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Behold, I will feed them distresses and make them drink gall-water,

relationship: close rejection of prophecy originating in the speaker's own heart
rationale: Jeremiah warns against prophetic words from the prophets' own hearts rather than the Lord's mouth. Ezekiel likewise condemns prophets speaking from their own heart while seeing nothing at all.
source_text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Do not listen to the prophets’ words, because they make a vision futile for themselves. They speak from their own heart and not from the Lord’s mouth.

target_units.text: “Son of man, prophesy against Israel’s prophets; you will prophesy and say to them, ‘Hear the Lord’s word!
Thus says the Lord: Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and see nothing at all!

relationship: close deceptive assurance of peace
rationale: Jeremiah condemns prophets promising peace and freedom from evils to those rejecting the Lord and following their own wishes. Ezekiel similarly says prophets misled the people by declaring peace where there was no peace.
source_text: They say to those rejecting the Lord’s word, You will have peace. To all who walk according to their own wishes, to everyone walking in the wandering of his heart, they said, No evils will come upon you.

target_units.text: Because they misled My people, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace, and this one builds a wall, and they coat it—if it is going to fall,

relationship: related access to the Lord's heavenly deliberation
rationale: Jeremiah asks who has stood in the Lord's standing place and seen or heard His word. Micaiah reports a vision of the Lord enthroned with heaven's army around Him and recounts the deliberation he heard; the narrative supplies an instance of claimed access without being quoted here verbatim.
source_text: Because who stood in the Lord’s standing place and saw His word? Who gave ear and heard?

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so—not I! Hear the Lord’s word—not so! I saw the Lord, the God of Israel, sitting on His throne, and all the army of heaven stood around Him, on His right and His left.
The Lord said, ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Remmath-gilead?’ One said this, and another said that.
A spirit came forward, stood before the Lord, and said, ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to it, ‘By what means?’
It said, ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will deceive him and indeed prevail. Go out and do so.’

relationship: close repeated announcement of swirling wrath upon the ungodly
rationale: Both announce anger proceeding from the Lord, describe its swirling movement and identify the ungodly as its destination. Chapter 23 also uses shaking and convulsion language.
source_text: Behold, a shaking comes from the Lord, and anger goes out into a convulsion; swirling, it will come upon the ungodly.

target_units.text: Because the Lord’s anger went out furious; swirling anger went out and will come upon the ungodly.

relationship: close repeated completion of the Lord's heart's undertaking
rationale: Both say the Lord's fury will not turn back until He acts on His heart's undertaking, followed by understanding at the end of the days. The supplied pronoun changes from they in chapter 23 to you in chapter 37.
source_text: And the Lord’s fury will no longer turn back until He does it and raises it up from His heart’s undertaking. At the end of the days they will understand these things.

target_units.text: The anger of the Lord’s fury will certainly not turn back until He acts and establishes His heart’s undertaking. At the end of the days you will know these things.

relationship: close denial that the prophets were sent by God
rationale: Jeremiah says the prophets ran though God did not send them and prophesied though He did not speak. Ezekiel similarly condemns those saying The Lord says although the Lord has not sent them.
source_text: I was not sending the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.

target_units.text: They see false things and divine vain things, those who say, ‘The Lord says,’ although the Lord has not sent them; and they began to establish a word.

relationship: related faithful ministry turning people from injustice
rationale: Jeremiah says prophets who truly stood before God and heard Him would have turned the people from evil practices. Malachi presents truthful priestly speech and the turning of many from injustice as the positive counterpart.
source_text: And if they had stood in My standing presence and listened to My words, they would have turned My people from their evil practices.

target_units.text: A law of truth was in his mouth, and injustice was not found on his lips. Directing his way in peace, he walked with Me and turned many back from injustice.

relationship: close affirmation that God is not far away
rationale: Jeremiah declares God drawing near and not far away. Paul's speech likewise says God is not far from each person and that in Him people live, move and exist; it does not turn Jeremiah's declaration into the question found in some other renderings.
source_text: I am a God drawing near, says the Lord, and not a God far away.

target_units.text: so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.
For in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are His offspring.’

relationship: related impossibility of escaping God's presence through place or darkness
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether a hidden person could escape God's sight and declares His filling heaven and earth. The psalm traces heaven, Hades, the far sea and darkness as places or conditions that cannot remove the speaker from God's presence.
source_text: If a person hides in hidden places, will I not see him? Do I not fill the heaven and the earth? says the Lord.

target_units.text: Where can I go from Thy Spirit, and where can I flee from Thy face?
If I ascend to heaven, Thou art there; if I descend into Hades, Thou art present.
if I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the sea’s farthest reaches,
indeed, even there Thy hand will guide me, and Thy right hand will hold me fast.
And I said, “Then darkness will trample me, and night is light in my delight.”
For darkness will not be dark from Thee, and night will be lit up like day; as its darkness, so also its light.

relationship: close affirmation that nothing is hidden from divine sight
rationale: Jeremiah denies that someone hiding in concealed places can remain unseen by God. Hebrews says no creature is hidden and everything lies exposed to His eyes, directly matching the visibility clause rather than merely the spatial imagery.
source_text: If a person hides in hidden places, will I not see him? Do I not fill the heaven and the earth? says the Lord.

target_units.text: And no created thing is hidden before Him, but all things are naked and laid open to His eyes, to whom we must give account.

relationship: close warning about dreams and false prophecy in God's name
rationale: Jeremiah reports prophets claiming dreams while speaking falsehood in His name. The later address to deportees warns against false prophets and dreams because the prophets speak unjust things in God's name without being sent.
source_text: I heard what the prophets speak, the false things they prophesy in My name, saying, I dreamed a dream.

target_units.text: Because thus said the Lord: Do not let the false prophets among you persuade you, and do not let your diviners persuade you. Do not listen to your dreams that you dream,
because they prophesy unjust things to you in My name, and I did not send them.

relationship: close prophetic claims proceeding from one's own heart
rationale: Jeremiah identifies the wishes of the prophets' own hearts as the source of their false prophesying. Ezekiel directs an oracle against women prophesying from their own heart, specifying a group the source does not separately name.
source_text: How long will it be in the heart of the prophets prophesying false things, and in their prophesying the wishes of their own heart?

target_units.text: And you, son of man, set your face firmly against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy against them,

relationship: related dreams threatening fidelity to God's commandments
rationale: Jeremiah accuses dream-telling prophets of planning forgetfulness of God's law, likening it to the fathers' forgetfulness through Baal. Deuteronomy warns against listening to a dreamer who urges service of other gods and instead commands adherence to the Lord's voice.
source_text: They plan to forget My law through their dreams, which each told his neighbor, just as their fathers forgot My name through Baal.

target_units.text: And if there arises among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and he gives you a sign or a wonder,
and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, whereof he spoke unto you, saying: Let us go and serve other gods, which you have not known,

you shall not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or unto that dreamer of dreams; for the Lord God tests you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
You shall walk after the Lord your God, and fear Him, and keep His commandments, and hearken unto His voice, and be joined unto Him.

relationship: related distinction between wheat and chaff with different referents
rationale: Jeremiah distinguishes the truthful divine word from dreams through the question of chaff and wheat. John's announcement pictures wheat gathered and chaff burned in coming judgment; the shared separation image does not identify Jeremiah's kinds of speech with the target's judged people.
source_text: Let the prophet in whom there is a dream tell his dream, and the one to whom My word comes tell My word in truth. What has chaff to do with wheat? So are My words, says the Lord.

target_units.text: His winnowing shovel is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clear His threshing floor and gather His wheat into the storehouse; but He will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

relationship: close comparison of God's words to consuming fire
rationale: Jeremiah 23 calls God's words blazing fire. The earlier oracle makes His words fire in the prophet's mouth and the people wood to be consumed, supplying an explicit application of the same image.
source_text: Are not My words like blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe cutting rock?

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: Because you spoke this utterance, behold, I have made My words fire in your mouth, and this people wood, and it will devour them.

relationship: related force of God's word pictured through cutting
rationale: Jeremiah pairs blazing fire with an axe cutting rock. Hebrews describes God's word as sharper than a sword and penetrating inward divisions; the instruments and objects differ, and Jeremiah's axe is not replaced with a hammer.
source_text: Are not My words like blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe cutting rock?

target_units.text: For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, penetrating as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

relationship: close condemnation of false prophecy without divine commission
rationale: Both deny that God sent or commanded prophets who claim to speak for Him. Chapter 23 stresses false dreams leading the people astray, while chapter 14 lists false visions, divinations, omens and choices of the heart.
source_text: Behold, I am against the prophets who prophesy false dreams, who told them and led My people astray by their lies and wanderings. I did not send or command them, and they will bring this people no benefit at all.

target_units.text: And the Lord said to me: The prophets prophesy false things in My name; I did not send them or command them or speak to them, because they prophesy false visions, divinations, omens, and their heart’s choices to you.

relationship: related accountability for spoken words
rationale: Jeremiah announces judgment on a person and household for using the forbidden Lord's burden expression. Jesus warns of accounting for idle words and condemnation by one's words; the target broadens the principle and does not prescribe Jeremiah's specific phrase prohibition.
source_text: And the prophet, priest, or people who say, The Lord’s burden—I will exact justice from that person and his household.

target_units.text: But I tell you that people will give account on the day of judgment for every idle word they speak.
For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

relationship: related request for a truthful report of the divine word
rationale: Jeremiah prescribes asking what the Lord answered and spoke. Eli likewise asks Samuel what word was spoken to him and demands that none be concealed, followed by Samuel's complete report; the narrative does not contain the burden controversy.
source_text: For this is what you will say, each to his neighbor and his brother: What did the Lord answer? What did the Lord speak?

target_units.text: He said, “What was the word spoken to you? Do not hide it from me. May God do these things to you, and add these things, if you hide from me a word of all the words spoken to you in your ears.”
Samuel reported all the words and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. He will do what is good before Him.”

relationship: related one's own words becoming the basis of adverse judgment
rationale: Jeremiah says a person's own word will become his burden after forbidding the disputed expression. Jesus likewise says people may be condemned by their own words; the comparison concerns responsibility for speech, not an identical use of the burden metaphor.
source_text: And do not name the Lord’s burden again, because a person’s own word will be his burden.

target_units.text: For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

relationship: related rejection of people together with their inherited place
rationale: Jeremiah announces casting down the people along with the city God gave them and their fathers. The temple oracle likewise threatens the place given to them and their fathers and the people's removal from God's presence, denying that inherited location guarantees safety.
source_text: therefore behold, I seize you and dash you down, along with the city I gave to you and your fathers,

target_units.text: I will also do to this house over which My name has been called, in which you have trusted, and to the place I gave you and your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
And I will throw you away from My presence, as I threw away your brothers, all Ephraim’s offspring.

relationship: close enduring disgrace that will not be forgotten
rationale: Both describe dishonor whose memory will not disappear. Chapter 20 applies this to the prophet's pursuers, while chapter 23 announces it upon those implicated in the burden controversy.
source_text: and I will put eternal reproach and eternal dishonor upon you, which will not be forgotten.

target_units.text: And the Lord is with me like a strong fighter. Therefore they pursued and could not understand; they were greatly shamed, because they did not understand their dishonors, which will never be forgotten.

relationship: close shared setting after Jeconiah and craftsmen left Jerusalem for exile
rationale: The fig vision is dated after Jeconiah and other groups, including craftsmen and prisoners, were deported from Jerusalem to Babylon. Jeremiah's letter to the Babylonian deportees is likewise situated after the departure from Jerusalem of the explicitly named King Jeconiah and groups including prisoners and craftsmen. The passages introduce different prophetic messages within this shared named setting.
source_text: The Lord showed me two baskets of figs lying before the Lord’s sanctuary, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, the rulers, craftsmen, prisoners, and rich people from Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon.

target_units.text: And these are the words of the document Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the elders of the deportation, the priests, and the false prophets—a letter to Babylon for the deportees and all the people—
after King Jeconiah, the queen, the eunuchs, and every free person, prisoner, and craftsman left Jerusalem,

relationship: related good and bad fruit imagery distinguishing human groups
rationale: Jeremiah's good and inedible figs become signs for the groups interpreted in the following oracle. Jesus contrasts good and evil fruit in a warning about recognizing false prophets; the signs serve different arguments and the target does not describe the fig baskets.
source_text: One basket had very good figs, like early figs; the other basket had very bad figs that could not be eaten because of their badness.

target_units.text: In the same way, every good tree bears good fruit, but the rotten tree bears evil fruit.
A good tree cannot bear evil fruit, nor can a rotten tree bear good fruit.
Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.
So then, you will recognize them by their fruits.

relationship: close visionary question asking Jeremiah what he sees
rationale: Both visions contain God's direct question What do you see, Jeremiah and the prophet's report of a visible object before its meaning is explained. The earlier object is a nut-wood staff, not the figs of this vision.
source_text: And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Jeremiah? I said: Figs. The good are exceedingly good, and the bad exceedingly bad; they cannot be eaten because of their badness.

target_units.text: The Lord’s word came to me, saying, What do you see, Jeremiah? I said, A nut-wood staff.
The Lord said to me, You have seen well, because I am watchful over My words to perform them.

relationship: related divine favor toward people already dispersed from Jerusalem
rationale: Jeremiah identifies the deportees as the good figs whom God will acknowledge for good. Ezekiel counters Jerusalem's inhabitants' claim against the dispersed and promises to gather the scattered back to Israel's land; the fig symbolism is distinctive to Jeremiah.
source_text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Like these good figs, so I will acknowledge Judah’s deportees, whom I have sent from this place to the Chaldeans’ land, for good things.

target_units.text: “Son of man, your brothers and the men of your captivity and the whole house of Israel have been brought to an end. To them Jerusalem’s inhabitants said, ‘Keep far from the Lord; the land has been given to us as an inheritance.’
Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: I will thrust them away into the nations and scatter them through all the earth, and I will be a little sanctuary for them in the countries where they may enter.’
Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: I will receive them from the nations and gather them from the countries where I scattered them, and I will give them the land of Israel.

relationship: close reversal from tearing down to building and planting
rationale: Jeremiah promises to rebuild and plant the returned deportees rather than tear down or pluck them out. The later oracle similarly contrasts God's prior watching to tear down and harm with His watching to build and plant.
source_text: And I will fix My eyes upon them for good things and restore them to this land for good things. I will rebuild them and certainly not tear them down, plant them and certainly not pluck them out.

target_units.text: And just as I watched over them to tear down and harm, so I will watch over them to build and plant, says the Lord.

relationship: close God-given heart and restored covenant relationship
rationale: Jeremiah promises a heart to know the Lord, return from the whole heart and the bond of My people and their God. Ezekiel promises a new heart and spirit enabling obedience and repeats the same people-and-God relationship.
source_text: And I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the Lord. They will be My people and I will be their God, because they will return to Me from their whole heart.

target_units.text: And I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you; and I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh, and give you a heart of flesh.
I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My ordinances, keep My judgments and do them.
You will dwell upon the land I gave your fathers. You will be My people, and I will be your God.

relationship: close handing over of Zedekiah and Jerusalem's remaining people
rationale: Jeremiah's bad-fig interpretation names Zedekiah, his nobles and the remnant in Jerusalem for handing over. The earlier siege oracle likewise names Zedekiah and the city's survivors being delivered to enemies; the bad-fig oracle additionally includes people dwelling in Egypt.
source_text: And like the bad figs that cannot be eaten because of their badness—thus says the Lord—so I will hand over Zedekiah king of Judah, his nobles, Jerusalem’s remnant left in this land, and those dwelling in Egypt.

target_units.text: And afterward—thus says the Lord—I will give Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants, and the people remaining in this city after death, famine, and sword into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives. They will cut them down with the sword’s edge. I will not spare them or have compassion on them.

relationship: close dispersion accompanied by proverbial disgrace among nations
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering into kingdoms and becoming a reproach, parable and curse wherever driven. Deuteronomy likewise predicts removal with rulers to an unknown nation and becoming a riddle, parable and tale among the nations.
source_text: And I will give them to scattering into all the earth’s kingdoms, and they will become a reproach, a parable, an object of hatred, and a curse in every place where I drove them out.

target_units.text: The Lord lead you, and your rulers whom you shall set over yourself, unto a nation which neither you nor your fathers have known; and there you shall serve other gods, wood and stone.
And there you shall become a riddle, and a parable, and a tale among all the nations whither the Lord shall lead you.

relationship: close divine judgments of famine, death and sword
rationale: Jeremiah names famine, death and sword against the condemned group until it disappears from the land. Ezekiel names those same three among four judgments against Jerusalem, adding harmful beasts and explicitly mentioning both people and livestock.
source_text: And I will send famine, death, and sword against them until they disappear from the land I gave them.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Even if I send My four evil retributions—sword, famine, evil beasts and death—against Jerusalem, to destroy human and livestock from her,
